newsitem.title: USA: Gov's report their states tightening budget belts.
newsitem.headline: Gov's report their states tightening budget belts.

text.p: States are "tightening their collective budget belts," allowing for only modest tax increases and striving for "trimmer, fitter" governments in fiscal 1997 and 1998 budgets, National Governors' Association reported in its annual review of state spending.

"The real news is that despite the fact that revenue growth has been relatively good, governors are not spending this money," Raymond Scheppach, executive director of the Governors' Association, said at a press briefing on the group's annual "Fiscal Survey of States."
Scheppach said states are expected to increase their general fund spending by only 4.5 percent in fiscal 1997 and 3.6 percent for fiscal 1998.
"This moderate spending increase would be the third lowest in the past 20 years," the governors reported.

"They are ratcheting down their rate of growth," Scheppach said. "They are continuing to make tax cuts and to build adequate but not huge reserves, and essentially, focusing on efficiency," Scheppach said.

"What voters are saying is that in terms of total spending and revenues, they like a little bit of tax cuts but not necessarily huge tax cuts. What they really want is more efficiency in state government," he said.
Scheppach said states are spending conservatively because of Congress' campaign to shift more social program spending out of Washington and its efforts to cut taxes.

He said Medicaid spending is growing at more moderate levels after years of double-digit growth rates. Congressional Budget Office now projects average annual growth grates of 7.7 percent through 2002, the governors' report says.

The governors said states are responding to a growing public distate for tax increases. About 25 states are proposing tax reductions, with the most signficant cuts in the personal income tax, the report says..

Concerned about a possible economic downturn in the next several years, states had end of year balances of over six percent in fiscal 1996 and 1997, which are expected to drop to just 5.1 percent in 1997, governors said.
Wall Street analysts believe that five percent is an adequate reserve, the report notes.
Regions are showing less variation in growth rates, the governors said.

They said personal income grew 6.3 percent in the Southeast and Southwest; 6.2 percent in the Far West and the Plains; 6.1 percent in the Rocky Mountain region; 5.4 percent in New England; and five percent in the Mid-Atlantic and Great Lakes regions.
